title: Partitioning by tenant
summary: Splitting a table so each tenant's rows live in their own partition with their own index, removing the post-filtering problem rather than mitigating it.
what: A LIST partition on tenant keeps each tenant's rows physically separate, and each partition carries its own vector index.
why: If an index contains only rows this role may see, there is nothing to post-filter away. The recall cliff disappears because the cause disappears.
how: The planner prunes partitions the query cannot match, so only permitted partitions are scanned. Passing the permitted tenant list as an explicit predicate enables that pruning at plan time.
in_this_project: Recommended for Phase 2 after the post-filtering measurements. Two things do different jobs here and it is worth being precise: row-level security is the correctness boundary, and the explicit tenant predicate is purely a performance hint. In the earlier synthetic measurement recall was identical with and without the predicate — the predicate never widened access — but plan-time pruning cut latency from 38.5 ms to 1.03 ms. The security test suite must therefore drop the predicate and still pass; that is what proves it is an optimisation and not the boundary.

left.title: Monolithic index
points: permitted rows may never be reached

limitations: Small tenants make per-partition indexes meaningless
Cross-tenant queries must touch many partitions

pitfalls: Treating the explicit predicate as the security boundary
Partitioning so finely that a partition holds fewer rows than ef_search

use: Tenant isolation matters and tenants are reasonably sized
avoid: Hundreds of tiny tenants; merge them into semantic groups first
